lines.text: Your arm now drives to an angle on Motion Magic while you hold a trigger. That command never ends on its own, so nothing in your code can say when the arm got there.
Arriving needs a tolerance, and picking it is a judgment call. A real sensor never sits perfectly still, so waiting for an exact match means waiting forever.
Then three small methods. Two only report: where the arm is right now, and where it's headed, read straight off the request you're already sending.
The third compares those two using your tolerance. Every routine you write later asks this question, so how close counts gets decided in one place.
An answer you can't see is hard to trust, so record it. Two lines at the top of the robot's constructor start a log file that runs for as long as the program does.
The second of those lines is the one people skip. It adds the driver station's side: whether the robot was enabled and what the sticks were doing.
The arm writes its own signals. Each one gets a name here, and those names are what you'll look for when you open the file.
Notice there's no unit conversion anywhere. The value goes in with its unit attached, and you choose degrees or rotations later, on the graph.
None of that runs until the robot calls it. One line for each mechanism, every loop, in a method that runs in every mode, so the log keeps going when your command doesn't.
Run it in hardware sim and move the arm twice. Then disable before you stop the program, or the last few entries never reach the file.
Open the newest log in AdvantageScope before you start the program again, because a file that hasn't been renamed yet gets deleted on the next start.
This is the check. The position catches up to the target, and the arrival signal turns true when they meet. A routine can wait on exactly that, which is the next lesson.
